entries.title: About the Course
entries.content: The focus of the course in this rotation is on answering the question, "Why do buildings stand up?"  The main text of that name offers the history of great monuments and the architectural technology that makes them possible. Famous buildings from 1800-1900 and 100 BC-350 AD are mentioned as well.

entries.title: Placement & Combining Tips
entries.content: Suitable for Grade 8 students with minimal adjustment if combining.

blocks.text: Connect back to the previous lesson. Take a minute (without looking ideally) to recall the ideas you read about last week.
Look at pictures from links or in the text of design features and/or famous buildings.
Various ways to narrate are assigned in the lessons. Because architecture is an especially visual subject, try to incorporate sketches frequently into your narrations and thoughts.
Discuss what you have learned and found interesting with a parent, teacher, or another student.
Plan time at the end of lesson or later in the afternoon to make additional drawings of buildings or features in a sketchbook and/or Book of Centuries.

These lessons are written directly to the student, but to assist them throughout the year, please read through this section and the lesson plans so you are familiar with the instructions and flow of the lessons. Accountability components are added to facilitate teacher/student discussion and growing independence. 

It is valuable for those in a classroom setting to also have a mix of lessons that students complete silently themselves and others read aloud and narrated together. Because of the visual elements of the course, it is especially suited to completing as a group. Classroom settings lend themselves well to additional discussion and sharing at the end of lessons after everyone has narrated either together or independently with their notebooks.

lessons.title: 30m Architecture: Grades 9-12 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Structures
⍞ Materials: Why Buildings Stand Up, notebook

➜ INTRO
Glance through the Contents page so you have a sense of what this book is going to be about. We don't often stop to think about why buildings stand up or consider all the different ways people have built in the past. As we learn about the science of construction, look around at the built structures in your area and see if you can begin to understand some of the secrets of their construction.

➜ READ
Preface and Ch.1 p.17-26

➜ NARRATE
Copy any diagrams or sketches that would be helpful to you in your notebook. Silently go over the reading in your mind. Sometimes it helps to talk aloud to yourself at first until you can silently narrate to yourself. With your sketches and written work, you will be creating an architecture notebook that will explore why buildings stand up. Be as creative as you like and enjoy the adventure!

➜ WRITE
Use the remaining time to write at least a paragraph about one aspect of the chapter that was especially interesting to you. For example, for this reading, you might want to write about the author's ideas about structure and function in architecture. What examples can you think of or what did you think about his ideas or what did his ideas make you ask questions about? 

➜ DISCUSS
Depending on your setting and schedule, discuss your thoughts with other students, your teacher, your parent, or another adult.

lessons.title: 30m Architecture: Grades 9-12 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
The Pyramids
⍞ Materials: Why Buildings Stand Up, notebook

➜ READ
Ch.2 p.27-38 

➜ NARRATE
Copy any diagrams or sketches that would be helpful to you in your notebook. Silently go over the reading in your mind. Sometimes it helps to talk aloud to yourself at first until you can silently narrate to yourself.  

➜ WRITE
Use the remaining time to write at least a paragraph about one aspect of the chapter that was especially interesting to you. For example, what about the construction process of the pyramids was most impressive or interesting to you? Explain in detail one aspect of the process. Because you narrated the whole reading silently to yourself, you now have a few moments to focus in on one part and give greater detail about that part.

➜ DISCUSS
Depending on your setting and schedule, discuss your thoughts that you wrote down or your answer to the following discussion prompt with other students, your teacher, your parent, or another adult.

• On p.28, Salvadori says, "Cultures are immortalized by monuments, which express their conception of the world, of life and death." What monuments today immortalize our conception of the world and of life and death as a culture?

Exam Week

➜ EXAMS 
Answer question(s) related to the course. 

Questions will come from:
Why Buildings Stand Up

terms.content: · Why Buildings Stand Up: Show your architecture notebook to your teacher. Write what you remember about pyramids, loads, materials, beams and columns, houses, or skyscrapers.

· Why Buildings Stand Up: Show your architecture notebook to your teacher. Write what you can about the Eiffel Tower, bridges, the Brooklyn Bridge, form-resistant structures, cathedrals, or the La Sagrada Familia.

· Why Buildings Stand Up: 1. Show your architecture notebook to your teacher. 2. Select a famous structure from the book — the Hagia Sophia, the Brooklyn Bridge, the Eiffel Tower, etc., and explain: (1) what structural problem the builders were solving, (2) what made their solution innovative, and (3) whether that same structure could be built today, and how.
